action_criteria.expected_evidence: Active denervation in bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral muscles with chronic neurogenic change in both hands, reduced median and ulnar CMAPs with normal conduction velocities and no conduction block, and normal sensory studies.
action_criteria.label: EMG and nerve conduction studies of the bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions to document lower motor neuron involvement and exclude conduction block and neuropathy
action_criteria.rationale: EMG/NCS confirms lower motor neuron involvement beyond the clinically affected muscles and excludes the main treatable mimics: multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block, demyelinating or sensorimotor neuropathy and myopathy. Gold Coast 2020 accepts EMG evidence of lower motor neuron dysfunction, and Awaji 2008 counts fasciculation potentials as active denervation in muscles with chronic neurogenic change.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilateral corticospinal tract T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and subtle motor-cortex low T2 signal (supportive only); no mass, hemorrhage, infarct or demyelinating lesion.
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude structural, vascular, demyelinating, inflammatory or neoplastic causes of the upper motor neuron or bulbar signs
action_criteria.rationale: MRI does not confirm ALS. It excludes brain and brainstem lesions that can cause upper motor neuron or bulbar signs; corticospinal tract signal change, when present, is supportive only.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No cervical or thoracic cord compression, cord signal abnormality or mass.
action_criteria.label: Spine MRI of the cervical and thoracic cord, and of the lumbosacral spine when lower limb signs need it, to exclude compressive myelopathy, radiculopathy and other cord lesions
action_criteria.rationale: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy with radiculopathy is the commonest structural mimic of combined upper and lower motor neuron signs in the limbs. Spine MRI excludes it, but incidental spondylosis does not explain bulbar signs or denervation in other regions and must not delay the ALS work-up.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: CK 1240 U/L (7.1x ULN); normal blood count, renal and liver function, calcium, thyroid function, vitamin B12, folate, ESR and CRP.
action_criteria.label: Blood tests for treatable mimics and a pre-treatment baseline: full blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes and calcium, CK, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and folate, ESR and CRP
action_criteria.rationale: These tests exclude metabolic, endocrine, nutritional and inflammatory mimics and give the liver and blood-count baseline needed before riluzole; phenotype-specific tests are added only when the case raises that mimic.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 91% predicted and SNIP 86 cmH2O, both normal: baseline for 3-monthly monitoring.
action_criteria.label: Baseline respiratory function (FVC and SNIP, with MIP where available) to stage respiratory muscle involvement and plan monitoring and NIV
action_criteria.rationale: Respiratory function does not diagnose ALS. Once ALS is supported it stages respiratory muscle weakness, sets the baseline for 3-monthly monitoring and identifies patients who need early referral for NIV.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Pathogenic C9orf72 hexanucleotide repeat expansion (more than 600 repeats); no pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant in SOD1, TARDBP, FUS or TBK1.
action_criteria.label: ALS gene panel (C9orf72 repeat expansion; SOD1, TARDBP, FUS and TBK1) after pre-test genetic counselling, once the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment is complete
action_criteria.rationale: Genetic testing does not make the diagnosis. It is offered with counselling to people with ALS because a pathogenic variant changes counselling for relatives and may open gene-targeted treatment or trials. The family history of his father's ALS makes a monogenic cause likely.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No regular medicines or alcohol to interact; liver transaminases before the first dose and on the monitoring schedule, stopping riluzole if ALT exceeds 5x ULN.
action_criteria.label: Check riluzole against the current medicines, alcohol use and liver function before the first dose, once the diagnosis is established
action_criteria.rationale: Riluzole is metabolised by CYP1A2 and can raise liver transaminases, so the medicine list, alcohol use and baseline liver function are reviewed before treatment. He takes no regular medicines and does not drink alcohol.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not treat ALS with corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange: they have no benefit.
Do not stop respiratory monitoring because the baseline values are normal.
required_recommendations: Make and explain the diagnosis of ALS by Gold Coast 2020 criteria: progressive bilateral hand weakness with upper motor neuron signs (brisk jaw jerk, brisk biceps and knee reflexes, bilateral Hoffman and Babinski signs, mildly spastic gait) and lower motor neuron involvement in the cervical region on examination and EMG, with active denervation also in bulbar, thoracic and lumbosacral muscles, with mimics excluded by MRI and blood tests; with the pathogenic C9orf72 expansion and his father's ALS this is C9orf72-associated familial ALS. Disclose it in a planned face-to-face discussion with the patient and family.

Repeat FVC and SNIP about every 3 months and ask at each review about orthopnoea, morning headache, daytime sleepiness and unrefreshing sleep, referring for NIV assessment when these appear or values fall.

Offer riluzole 50 mg twice daily. Measure liver transaminases before the first dose, monthly for 3 months, every 3 months for the rest of the first year and periodically thereafter; stop riluzole if ALT exceeds 5x the upper limit of normal, and ask the patient to report any febrile illness so that neutropenia can be excluded.

Refer to a specialist ALS multidisciplinary team (neurologist, specialist nurse, respiratory, speech and language therapy, dietetics, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and palliative care), reviewed about every 2 to 3 months, with an early, patient-paced discussion of advance care planning.
Provide post-test genetic counselling about the C9orf72 expansion, including the frontotemporal dementia risk.
Offer counselling to his first-degree relatives, each of whom has a 50% chance of carrying the expansion, with predictive testing only after counselling.
Perform baseline cognitive and behavioural screening (for example ECAS) because of the C9orf72-associated frontotemporal dementia risk.
Discuss eligibility for C9orf72-targeted clinical trials at the specialist centre.

avoided_actions.rationale: ALS is a motor-neuron disease without cortical electrical signature; EEG has no diagnostic role and adds cost without benefit.
ECG is unrelated to motor neuron disease and not part of the standard ALS workup absent specific cardiac symptoms or pre-medication QTc checks.
Echocardiography is unrelated to ALS diagnosis; no indication absent comorbid cardiac disease.
Cardiac monitoring has no role in ALS diagnostic workup.
MRI is the standard structural study for ALS workup; head CT adds no diagnostic value and exposes the patient to ionizing radiation.
Amyloid PET has no role in ALS diagnosis (motor-neuron rather than amyloid pathology) and carries a high cost.
DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic integrity; it has no role in ALS, which spares the dopaminergic system.
FDG-PET has no established diagnostic role in ALS and adds substantial cost.

key_clinical_evidence: Gold Coast 2020: ALS needs progressive motor impairment with upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least one body region, or lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least two, after other diseases are excluded. Here: brisk jaw jerk, brisk biceps and knee reflexes, bilateral Hoffman and Babinski signs and a mildly spastic gait with lower motor neuron involvement in the cervical region, with active denervation also in bulbar, thoracic and lumbosacral muscles.
EMG lower motor neuron evidence is chronic neurogenic change with active denervation; by Awaji 2008 fasciculation potentials count as active denervation in a muscle with chronic neurogenic change.
Normal motor conduction velocities without conduction block argue against multifocal motor neuropathy, and normal sensory responses argue against a sensorimotor neuropathy or SBMA.

CK 1240 U/L is 7.1x ULN, higher than usual in ALS: consider a myopathic contributor clinically, while the neurogenic EMG pattern with fasciculations and upper motor neuron signs argues against a primary myopathy.

FVC 91% predicted and SNIP 86 cmH2O are normal and set the baseline for 3-monthly monitoring. AAN 2009 markers that prompt NIV discussion are orthopnoea, FVC below 50% predicted, SNIP below 40 cmH2O, MIP weaker than -60 cmH2O or abnormal overnight oximetry; NIV prolongs survival and improves quality of life (Bourke 2006).

The C9orf72 hexanucleotide repeat expansion is the commonest genetic cause of both ALS and frontotemporal dementia; with his father's ALS it makes this C9orf72-associated familial ALS. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with age-dependent, incomplete penetrance, so each first-degree relative has a 50% chance of carrying it, predictive testing follows counselling, and cognitive and behavioural screening is part of his baseline.

sequence_constraints.reason: Genetic testing follows the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment and pre-test counselling; it does not make the diagnosis.
Riluzole is considered only after the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment supports ALS.

findings.finding: Bilateral FDI and APB: fibrillations +3, positive sharp waves +2, large amplitude polyphasic MUPs (amplitude >4 mV, duration >16ms), markedly reduced recruitment. Bilateral cervical paraspinals: fibrillations +2.
Bilateral tibialis anterior: fibrillations +1, fasciculations. Right vastus lateralis: fasciculations +1.
Median, ulnar, radial and sural sensory responses: normal amplitudes and conduction velocities.

Bilateral median motor: CMAP amplitudes markedly reduced (right 1.8 mV, left 2.4 mV; reference >4.5 mV). Normal distal latencies and conduction velocities. No conduction block. No temporal dispersion. Bilateral ulnar motor: CMAP amplitudes reduced, normal distal latencies and conduction velocities, no conduction block across the elbow or in the forearm. Peroneal and tibial motor: normal CMAP amplitudes, distal latencies and conduction velocities, no conduction block.

specialized_test.impression: 1. Active denervation (fibrillation potentials) in bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral muscles, with chronic neurogenic change (large polyphasic motor unit potentials, markedly reduced recruitment) in both first dorsal interossei and abductor pollicis brevis muscles; complex fasciculation potentials in the tongue and fasciculations in tibialis anterior and vastus lateralis. 2. Reduced median and ulnar CMAP amplitudes with normal distal latencies and conduction velocities; no conduction block or temporal dispersion in any nerve tested. 3. Normal sensory conduction studies. Findings indicate a widespread disorder of anterior horn cells, consistent with a motor neuron disease.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive bilateral hand weakness and fasciculations over 8 months

family_history: Father: ALS diagnosis at age 62 (died 2 years after diagnosis)

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. C is a 47-year-old software developer who presents with an 8-month history of progressive bilateral hand weakness and widespread muscle fasciculations. His father was diagnosed with ALS at age 62 and died within 2 years; this family history has made Mr. C hypervigilant to any neurological symptoms. He first noticed subtle difficulty typing quickly on his keyboard approximately 8 months ago and attributed it to repetitive strain injury. However, over the following months, the weakness progressed to involve both hands more symmetrically, and he began to notice widespread muscle twitching in his arms and thighs. He is deeply distressed about the possibility of familial ALS given his father's diagnosis. He has no history of heavy metal exposure, toxic exposures, or recent infections. He has never used tobacco or alcohol. He works from home and his sedentary lifestyle has made any functional decline more apparent to him. He reports no dysphagia, dysarthria, or respiratory symptoms at this time. He has no cognitive changes. He has been extensively researching ALS genetics and specifically requests testing for inherited forms. The progression has been relentless over the 8-month course with no periods of improvement or stabilization.

neurological_exam.motor: Bilateral hand weakness, right greater than left. Right thenar and hypothenar atrophy. Fasciculations visible bilateral deltoids, forearms, and thighs.
